clue.text: Remove restrictions on students I caught in dare

indicators.note: something caught in a thing is held inside it, so the earlier letters go inside the later ones

parts.note: to dare someone is to defy them
a class is a group of students
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone dares to lift the rules on a group of students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught in dare' reads as a schoolboy caught on a dare; 'dare' is in fact the outer word, broken open to take the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Declassifying secret documents lifts the official limits on who may see them, a close synonym for removing restrictions.

clue.text: Not smart to send up bishop with slander

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending something up turns it upside down, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: mud is slander, as in 'throwing mud' at someone
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: It is unwise to mock a bishop while also slandering him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send up' reads as mocking, but in a down clue it lifts the letters of MUD so they read DUM; the bishop is listed first but goes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumb is an informal word for stupid, so it means lacking intelligence or not clever.

clue.text: In report, betray group of spies

indicators.note: a report is something spoken and heard, so the word is identified by its sound

parts.note: to sell someone out is to betray them

explanation.surface: A news report tells of someone betraying a spy ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sell' as in 'sell out' means betray; the soft C makes the spy group's word sound identical.
explanation.definitionFit: A cell is a small secret unit within a larger espionage or terrorist network, operating independently of others.

clue.text: Assume it's suitable

definitions.meaning: first meaning, a verb: to take for oneself, as in assuming control
second meaning, an adjective: fitting or proper

explanation.walkthrough: The verb (stress on the last syllable) and the adjective are spelt the same but pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: To appropriate is to take possession of something, like assuming power; as an adjective it means fitting the occasion.

clue.text: Given investment, son made more comfortable

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
shoes that are worn in have been made comfortable by use

explanation.surface: A son's financial investment has made his life more comfortable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investment' here is not money but the formal installing of someone in an office.
explanation.definitionFit: Investiture is the ceremony of installing an official, who is formally sworn in by taking an oath of office.

clue.text: Service provided by personal digital assistant?

definitions.text: Service provided by personal digital assistant?

parts.words: Service provided by personal digital assistant?
parts.note: surface reading: a feature offered by a pocket electronic organiser, a PDA
setter's reading: digits are also toes, so this is a personal helper who works on your toes, like a masseur

explanation.walkthrough: PDA was the name for handheld organisers before smartphones; 'digital' is the trap, since toes are digits too.
explanation.definitionFit: A massage of the feet and toes is a pampering service a personal attendant could offer to a client.

clue.text: Public transport in shopping centre that's revolutionary

indicators.note: a revolution is a turning round, so the letters are turned to run backwards

parts.note: a mart is a market or shopping centre

explanation.surface: A new kind of public transport runs through a shopping mall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests novelty, but it is the signal to read the word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tram is a passenger vehicle running on rails along city streets, a common form of public transit.

clue.text: Narrating another reckoning

definitions.meaning: second meaning: counting again, as in an election re-count

explanation.walkthrough: The same letters read as 'recounting' (telling) and 're-counting' (counting a second time).
explanation.definitionFit: To recount is to tell a story in detail, and to re-count votes is to add them up once more.

clue.text: Discharge warning signal somewhere in the Alps

parts.note: matter is pus, the discharge from a wound
a horn is sounded as a warning

explanation.surface: An avalanche warning is fired off somewhere in the mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discharge' looks like a verb, as in firing a flare, but it is the noun meaning pus.
explanation.definitionFit: The Matterhorn is a famous pyramid-shaped peak on the Swiss-Italian border, one specific place in that mountain range.

clue.text: Poor plasma set is quite unsuitable

indicators.note: to set something is to arrange it, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shoddy plasma television is just not fit for purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'set' (as in TV set) does the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Malapropos, from French, describes a remark or action that is inappropriate or ill-timed for the occasion.

clue.text: Seen in royal racecourse, topless Northerner

indicators.note: without a top, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: Ascot is the racecourse in Berkshire with the Royal Ascot meeting

explanation.surface: A man from the north is spotted shirtless at a posh race meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is an English racecourse associated with the royal family; drop its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland lies in the north of Britain, so a person from there is a northerner from an English viewpoint.

clue.text: Regretfully rue cosy hut? No, it's a grand home

indicators.note: regret suggests things going wrong, so these letters are disturbed into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sadly regrets a snug little hut, having moved into a stately mansion instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rue' is part of the fodder, not a hint at regret; the adverb does the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: A country house is a large rural mansion, typically the estate residence of a wealthy or aristocratic family.

clue.text: Awkward situations, greetings

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a 'fine how-do-you-do' is a mess or awkward state of affairs
second meaning: the formal words said on being introduced

explanation.walkthrough: 'A fine how-do-you-do' is an old British idiom for a predicament.
explanation.definitionFit: The formal salutation exchanged at introductions doubles, in idiom, as a word for an embarrassing muddle or predicament.

clue.text: Householders, horrible horsewomen

indicators.note: something horrible is a mess, so the letters that follow are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The residents complain about some unpleasant female riders.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the riders is reused; 'horrible' sits between definition and fodder as the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A householder owns or occupies a house, so it is a close synonym for people owning their own property.

clue.text: Agent is bitter about shows

parts.note: a rep, short for representative, is a sales agent
to resent something is to be bitter about it

explanation.surface: A theatrical agent is resentful about the productions on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shows' looks like a noun about theatre, but it is a verb meaning depicts.
explanation.definitionFit: A painting that represents a scene depicts or portrays it, the same sense as showing it.

clue.text: Deliveries proceed quickly in storm

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six deliveries by one bowler
to run is to move quickly

explanation.surface: Parcels are rushed through despite bad weather.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket is a bat-and-ball game where a bowler delivers the ball six times per over. 'Storm' is a verb, as in storming a castle.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops who storm a position overrun it, swarming over and occupying it by force.

clue.text: Dog suppressing disgusted expression in entrance

indicators.note: to suppress something is to hold it down within, so one piece is kept inside another

parts.note: a bitch is a female dog
'ew' is an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: A dog stifles a look of disgust while standing in the doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' looks like a doorway, but it is the verb (en-TRANCE), meaning to put under a spell.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to fill them with wonder as if under a spell, which is to cast a charm upon them.

clue.text: Early aviator regarded highly as redoubtable trailblazer, primarily?

definitions.text: Early aviator regarded highly as redoubtable trailblazer, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so only the leading letter of each word is used

parts.words: Early aviator regarded highly as redoubtable trailblazer
parts.note: the initial letters of these seven words

explanation.surface: A pioneering pilot of the past is celebrated as a formidable pathfinder.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer and also spells it with its first letters, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Amelia Earhart was a pioneering American pilot, the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, in 1932.

clue.text: Small-time Everyman's a pitiful character

parts.note: tiny means small
T is the abbreviation for time
the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I, and 'Everyman's' as I'M

explanation.surface: The setter is confessing to being a pathetic small-time figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small-time' looks like one word, but it splits into small and time. 'Everyman's' is the setter saying I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny Tim is the sickly crippled boy in Dickens's A Christmas Carol, a figure meant to arouse pity.

clue.text: Male, hairy: to him it's a salutation!

definitions.text: Male, hairy: to him it's a salutation!

parts.note: surface reading: a description of a hirsute man
setter's reading: swap the initial sounds and 'male, hairy' becomes 'Hail, Mary', a prayer of greeting; the clue asks who would say it that way

explanation.walkthrough: William Archibald Spooner, an Oxford don, was famous for swapping the starts of words, which gave the spoonerism its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The reverend gave his name to the slip of the tongue, so he is the man who might greet with 'Male, hairy'.

clue.text: Messiaen abruptly composed description of blue-eyed cat

indicators.note: ending abruptly means stopping short, so the final letter is cut off
to compose is to put together in a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the composer's name with its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: The composer Messiaen hurriedly wrote a piece portraying a blue-eyed cat.
explanation.walkthrough: Olivier Messiaen was a French composer, so 'composed' fits the surface while signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Siamese cats are a breed known for striking blue eyes, so the breed name describes such a cat.

clue.text: Land one time in blazing row with Massenet about second piece in Manon

indicators.note: about means around, so one set of letters wraps around another
something blazing is in a heated, chaotic state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the second piece of a word is its second letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the second letter of the opera's title

explanation.surface: Massenet has a furious quarrel during his opera Manon.
explanation.walkthrough: Manon is an opera by Massenet, which disguises it as part of the story. 'One time' means formerly: the country dropped 'Western' from its name in 1997.
explanation.definitionFit: Samoa, a Pacific island nation, was officially called Western Samoa until 1997, so it is a country under its former name.

clue.text: A little man, one who hasn't been named?

definitions.text: A little man, one who hasn't been named?

indicators.note: a little of something is only part of it, so the letters come from inside the words

parts.note: found running across the two words

explanation.surface: A short man is someone whose name nobody knows.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both describes the answer and holds it: 'a little' of 'man, one'. The question mark flags that double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is short for anonymous, the label given to an author or person whose name is unknown.

clue.text: The French starters of snails — succulent? Not so much

parts.note: le is French for 'the' (masculine singular)

indicators.note: starters are what come first, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: French starters of snails: are they juicy? Not really.
explanation.walkthrough: Snails (escargots) are a classic French starter, which makes 'starters' look like the dish course rather than first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Less means a smaller amount, so it is the comparative of little, equal in sense to a lesser quantity.

clue.text: Sea eagle's gross, we're told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the word is judged by sound

parts.note: to gross is to earn before deductions

explanation.surface: Apparently the sea eagle is disgusting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gross' reads as an adjective (disgusting) but is the verb meaning to earn in total.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed eagle, a large bird of prey of coasts, a crossword regular.

clue.text: What ten dancers will hold: an audience?

indicators.note: to hold something is to contain it, so the letters are found inside the words

parts.note: found running across the three words

explanation.surface: A riddle: what will a troupe of ten dancers attract, a crowd?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'hold' is not about the dancers holding something but the words concealing it.
explanation.definitionFit: An attendance is the body of people present at an event, the same as the audience watching a performance.

clue.text: Special Forces getting hot in military gear

parts.note: the SAS (Special Air Service) is the British Army's special forces regiment
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Commandos overheat in their heavy combat kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal, but nothing goes inside anything here; it just links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is a band of cloth worn over the shoulder or round the waist as part of a dress uniform.

clue.text: Characters in R&B, &c.?

parts.note: surface reading: the people in a rhythm-and-blues scene, and so on
setter's reading: the typographical characters literally printed here are the '&' signs

explanation.walkthrough: '&c.' is an old way of writing etc., itself using the symbol; 'characters' means typed symbols, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: The '&' sign standing for 'and' is a typographic character, and there are two of them in the clue.
